title: Finch: conversational finance data agent in Slack
problem: Finance analysts lose time locating datasets and writing complex SQL; requests to data science take hours or days.
depth: Detailed architecture with evaluation approach; no quantitative results published
technologies_stated: Slack SDK and Slack AI Assistant APIs
Uber Generative AI Gateway (self-hosted and third-party LLMs)
facts: The agent runs inside Slack using the Slack SDK and AI Assistant APIs, with live status updates.
LangGraph coordinates a supervisor that routes requests to specialised sub-agents such as a SQL writer and a document reader.
Models are reached through an internal generative AI gateway so they can be swapped; both self-hosted and third-party LLMs are used.
Data is exposed as curated single-table data marts; an OpenSearch index holds column names, values and aliases for fuzzy matching of filter values.
The SQL writer checks the user's permissions before running a query; RBAC limits access to sensitive financial data.
Evaluation compares query results against golden queries, tests supervisor routing on ambiguous intents, runs end-to-end simulations and regression re-runs before prompt or model changes.
Sub-agents run in parallel and common metrics are pre-fetched to cut latency.
The authors acknowledge hallucination risk and plan on-demand expert validation of answers.
interpretations: Comparing result sets rather than SQL text tolerates equivalent queries but needs stable reference data; it can mask semantic mistakes when both queries share the same wrong filter.
Simplifying schemas into single-table marts moves complexity from the model into data engineering, trading flexibility for reliability.
unknown: Quantified accuracy, latency, adoption or time savings
How RBAC is implemented and how identity reaches the data sources

review_exercise: Finch states permission checks occur before query execution but not how identity propagates. List three ways a delegated agent could exceed a user's data rights and the control that closes each.
lessons: Constrain the data the model sees before tuning the model.
Evaluate agents per component and end to end, and regression-test before every prompt or model change.
Plan human validation for decisions that matter, because the authors themselves cite hallucination risk.
adaptation: For SAP CX analytics (sales or service KPIs), the same pattern maps to BDC data products as the curated layer and Joule Studio or a BTP agent as the supervisor; identity propagation then becomes the main design question (see T2.4.2). This mapping is independent analysis.
